Narwhals’ Legendary Tusks Are More Than Just Decoration
The Arctic unicorn.

Narwhals are famous for their long, spiraled tusks, which are actually elongated canine teeth, often growing over 8 feet long. These tusks contain millions of nerve endings and are highly sensitive to touch, temperature, and pressure.
They are believed to help males assert dominance and attract mates. Tusks may also serve as sensory organs to detect changes in the environment, providing an evolutionary edge.
Tusks’ multifunctionality underscores the unique adaptation of narwhals to harsh Arctic environments. The tusk is not just ornamental but integral to survival and social interaction.
Some narwhals have two tusks, but it is extremely rare.

Narwhals Can Dive Over a Mile Deep
Deep-sea adventurers.
Narwhals are among the deepest-diving marine mammals, reaching depths of over 1,500 meters. They can stay submerged for more than 25 minutes using oxygen stored in muscles and blood.
These extreme dives allow them to access squid, fish, and other prey that other predators cannot reach. Their adaptations include slowed heart rates and collapsible lungs to manage pressure.
Deep diving gives narwhals a competitive advantage in hunting and reduces predation risks. It highlights extraordinary physiological evolution in Arctic mammals.
Narwhals sometimes dive multiple times a day to such depths in search of food.

Narwhals Use Echolocation to Hunt in Total Darkness
Arctic sonar specialists.
Narwhals produce clicks, whistles, and pulsed sounds to navigate and locate prey in dark, ice-covered waters. Echolocation helps them detect obstacles, prey movement, and other pod members.
This adaptation allows hunting in conditions where sunlight never penetrates, giving narwhals access to deep-water prey. Echolocation is essential for pod coordination and survival.
It demonstrates the evolution of sophisticated sensory systems for extreme environments. Echolocation precision is critical for avoiding predators and obstacles.
Narwhals can identify prey location down to a few centimeters using echolocation.
